fields.definition: A Steinberg Cubase/Nuendo transport mode that decouples the project cursor and cycle range from the play/stop state, so the cursor can be repositioned and the left/right locators moved freely while playback keeps running.
fields.plain_english: A play mode in Cubase that lets you jump the playback line to a new spot without stopping the music. It is like being able to skip around a song while it keeps playing.
fields.purpose_function: It removes the stop-and-restart step from looping and auditioning, so an engineer can move the cursor or resize a loop on the fly and hear the change right away.
fields.practical_application: An engineer turns it on to reposition the cursor or resize the cycle range while a track keeps playing, quickly checking edits or comping takes without halting playback.
common_mistakes: Confusing Dynamic Transport with normal transport, then being surprised that the cursor moves without stopping playback
Assuming it is a Pro Tools or Logic feature; it is specific to Steinberg Cubase and Nuendo
Leaving it enabled and accidentally repositioning the cursor in the middle of a take
scenario_contexts: Auditioning several sections of a mix in a row without stopping playback
Adjusting a loop range on the fly while comping vocal takes
Jumping quickly between song sections during an editing session in Cubase

sources: Steinberg Cubase Pro Operation Manual (Dynamic Transport)

fields.definition: A list-style DAW editor that shows each recorded event, such as MIDI notes, controllers, program changes or automation points, as a separate line so the exact numeric properties of any single event, including position, type, pitch, velocity and value, can be inspected and edited.
fields.plain_english: A tool that shows every note and control message in your track as a list you can edit. It is like a spreadsheet of everything the music does, with one row per event.
fields.purpose_function: It gives precise numeric control over individual events that are hard to grab accurately in a graphical view, such as fixing one note's timing or a single controller value.
fields.practical_application: A technician opens it to correct an exact note length, delete a stray controller message, or change one event's velocity that would be fiddly to edit by dragging in the piano roll.
common_mistakes: Confusing the event editor with the piano roll; both change the same data but in different views
Editing raw controller numbers without knowing which controller number does what
Deleting note-off or controller events and leaving stuck notes or hanging values
scenario_contexts: Fixing the exact start position of a single MIDI note
Removing a duplicate program-change message from a track
Checking the precise velocity values of a recorded drum part

sources: Apple Logic Pro User Guide (Event List editor)

fields.definition: The stream of MIDI Continuous Controller messages a moving expression pedal produces, most commonly Controller 11 (Expression) but often assignable to other controllers, carrying values from 0 to 127 that a DAW records and plays back as controller or automation data.
fields.plain_english: The control messages a foot pedal sends as you rock it, usually to change volume or an effect. Your DAW saves this as a moving value from 0 to 127, like a dimmer for sound.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a performer shape a sound continuously with the foot, freeing the hands, and gives the DAW a recordable controller stream for expression such as volume swells, wah or effect depth.
fields.practical_application: A technician assigns the pedal to the correct controller, records its moves along with a performance, then edits the resulting controller lane to smooth or fix the expression.
common_mistakes: Assuming every expression pedal sends Controller 11; many are assignable and may default to a different controller
Confusing an expression pedal, which is a variable controller, with a sustain footswitch, which is on/off
Recording jumpy data from a mis-calibrated pedal and not smoothing it afterward
scenario_contexts: Recording volume swells on a synth pad with a foot pedal
Controlling wah or filter cutoff hands-free during a guitar or keyboard take
Mapping a pedal to a plug-in parameter and capturing its movement as automation

sources: MIDI Association, MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification (Control Change, Controller 11 Expression)
Steinberg Cubase Operation Manual (MIDI controller data)

fields.definition: The practice of streaming recorded audio to a hard disk drive housed outside the computer and connected by an interface such as USB, Thunderbolt or FireWire, keeping the record media separate from the system/boot drive.
fields.plain_english: Recording your audio onto a separate hard drive that plugs into your computer, instead of the built-in drive. This gives the recording its own space, so the computer runs more smoothly.
fields.purpose_function: It separates audio streaming from the operating-system and application load, which cuts disk contention, supports reliable track counts, and makes a whole project portable between systems.
fields.practical_application: An engineer records and plays back sessions from a dedicated external drive, then unplugs it to move the full project to another studio or keep it as a working copy.
common_mistakes: Recording large sessions to a slow, bus-powered USB drive and hitting audio dropouts
Using one drive for both the system and audio, overloading the disk on high track counts
Treating the working external drive as a backup; a working drive is not a backup
scenario_contexts: Tracking a live multitrack session to a dedicated external drive
Carrying a project between two studios on one portable drive
Freeing the internal drive by streaming audio playback from an external disk

sources: Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide (hard drive requirements / audio drives)

fields.definition: Streaming recorded audio to a solid-state drive connected outside the computer, typically over USB 3, USB-C or Thunderbolt, which has no moving parts and offers high sustained transfer rates and low access latency for large track counts.
fields.plain_english: Recording your audio onto an external solid-state drive, which has no spinning parts and is very fast. It is like swapping a slow disk for quick flash memory, so many tracks record without stutter.
fields.purpose_function: It provides fast, shock-resistant, low-latency storage for recording and playback, supporting higher track counts and denser sessions than a spinning disk while keeping media off the system drive.
fields.practical_application: An engineer uses a bus-powered external SSD to track high-channel-count sessions on location, knowing it tolerates movement far better than a hard disk during transport.
common_mistakes: Assuming any USB enclosure delivers full SSD speed; a slow bridge chip or a USB 2 port throttles it
Running the SSD nearly full, which can slow sustained write speed during recording
Trusting a single SSD as the only copy of a session, since flash failure can be sudden; always keep a backup
scenario_contexts: Recording a large location session onto a rugged bus-powered SSD
Running a high-track-count mix directly from an external SSD
Choosing an SSD over a hard drive for reliable playback during a mobile shoot

sources: Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide (storage requirements)

fields.definition: The process of identifying audio, MIDI or session files whose data has been damaged or altered, for example by incomplete writes, media faults or transfer errors, typically by comparing a stored checksum or hash against a freshly computed one or by a program's own file-validation routines flagging unreadable data.
fields.plain_english: Checking whether a saved file has been damaged and can no longer be read correctly. It works like a fingerprint: if the file's fingerprint changes, you know something went wrong.
fields.purpose_function: It catches damaged files early, before a corrupt take or session is trusted in a project or archive, so the file can be replaced from a backup while a good copy still exists.
fields.practical_application: A technician runs a checksum or a DAW's verify function after copying a session, and if a file fails the check they restore it from another copy instead of opening the bad file.
common_mistakes: Assuming a file that copied without an error message is intact; only a checksum or verify pass proves it
Detecting corruption but having no backup to restore the file from
Ignoring early read errors on a drive until more files are lost
scenario_contexts: Verifying a session after copying it to an archive drive
Tracking down why one audio file plays back as noise or silence
Checking delivered files against supplied checksums before a mastering session

sources: IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (checksums / fixity)
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (backup and archiving)

fields.definition: The ongoing checking of stored files over time to confirm they have not changed or degraded, done by periodically recomputing each file's checksum and comparing it to a recorded value (a fixity check), so that silent corruption or accidental modification is detected.
fields.plain_english: Regularly re-checking your stored files to make sure they have not changed or gone bad over time. If a file's fingerprint no longer matches, you know it needs restoring from a backup.
fields.purpose_function: It catches silent data rot and accidental or unauthorized changes in an archive, so long-term project and master files stay trustworthy across years of storage.
fields.practical_application: A technician keeps a checksum manifest of an archived project and re-runs fixity checks on a schedule, restoring any file that fails from a redundant copy.
common_mistakes: Confusing a one-time copy verification with ongoing monitoring; integrity must be re-checked over time
Storing the checksum list on the same drive as the files, so one drive failure loses both
Assuming a single archive copy is safe without periodic checks and a second copy
scenario_contexts: Maintaining a long-term archive of finished album masters
Scheduling periodic fixity checks on a studio's project library
Detecting bit rot on aging backup drives before a restore is needed

sources: IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (fixity / integrity checking)
AES technical documentation on digital audio archiving

fields.definition: A backup that copies the complete set of selected data, all files in a session, project or drive, in a single operation, as opposed to an incremental or differential backup that copies only what has changed since a previous backup.
fields.plain_english: A backup that copies everything at once, not just the parts that changed. It is like photocopying a whole notebook instead of only the newest page.
fields.purpose_function: It provides one self-contained copy from which everything can be restored, simplifying recovery because no earlier backups are needed to rebuild the data set.
fields.practical_application: An engineer makes a full backup of a finished project to an archive drive, so the entire session can be restored later from that single copy.
common_mistakes: Confusing a full backup with an incremental one and assuming a partial copy holds everything
Keeping the only full backup on a drive stored next to the original, so one accident destroys both
Never testing a restore, then finding the backup is incomplete or unreadable when it is needed
scenario_contexts: Archiving a completed album project to two separate drives
Making a complete copy of a session before a major edit or plug-in change
Backing up an entire working drive before reformatting or upgrading a system

sources: Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (backup and archiving)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects

fields.definition: The timing resolution to which edits and moves align in a DAW timeline, such as bars, beats, note divisions like 1/4, 1/8 or 1/16, or absolute units like frames or milliseconds, so that when snapping is enabled events jump to the nearest point on this grid.
fields.plain_english: The setting that decides where your edits snap to on the timeline, such as every beat or every 1/16 note. It works like the lines on ruled paper, keeping your edits lined up instead of landing anywhere.
fields.purpose_function: It keeps edits musically and rhythmically aligned, so cutting, moving and looping stay in time with the project tempo without constant manual nudging.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets the snap value to match the task, using a coarse value like 1/4 for arranging blocks, a fine value like 1/16 for detailed edits, or turning it off for free placement.
common_mistakes: Leaving snap on a coarse value and wondering why edits jump away from where they were dropped
Confusing the grid/snap value with quantize; snap constrains manual edits, while quantize moves recorded notes
Editing freely played material to the grid until it feels stiff and mechanical
scenario_contexts: Setting snap to 1/16 to line up a chopped drum loop
Turning snap off to nudge a clip into a natural-feeling spot
Using bar snapping to move whole song sections cleanly

sources: Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide (Grid mode / Nudge)
Ableton Live Reference Manual (Grid and Snapping)
